The United Arab Emirates currently operates one crude export pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz and announced earlier this year that it was building a second. A third pipeline is reportedly being planned to further expand crude capacity and reroute energy flows around Hormuz, reducing exposure to Iranian disruption and weakening Tehran's leverage over the critical maritime chokepoint. Bloomberg reported Wednesday morning that Abu Dhabi’s state-owned energy giant, Abu Dhabi National Oil Co., is weighing plans for a third pipeline from the UAE’s western coast to Fujairah on its eastern coast that could supply Asian customers and bypass Hormuz. "Adnoc has been telling some customers in Asia about the pipeline, other people familiar with the matter said. The plans haven’t been finalized and could still change, including the route, a number of the people said," the outlet reported. The new pipeline would build on the UAE's existing pipeline, which has operated since 2012 and stretches 252 miles from Habshan in Abu Dhabi to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman. That pipeline has a capacity of 1.5 million barrels a day, expandable to 1.8 million. Earlier this year, the UAE announced the West-East Pipeline, expected to begin operations in 2027 and double export capacity through Fujairah. Notably, Fujairah sits outside the Hormuz chokepoint, allowing tankers to load crude without entering the Persian Gulf. An ADNOC spokesperson responded to the outlet's request for comment: “We have advised Bloomberg that this report is not accurate and purely speculative.” Beyond the UAE, the biggest story of the year has been other US-allied Gulf countries expanding pipeline routes around Hormuz, including Saudi Arabia , while Kuwait is proposing new pipelines. body: Copper prices plunged to a three-month low this week as fears over the AI boom spread from technology stocks into commodities. On Tuesday, copper fell 3.2% to $13,883 per ton on the London Metal Exchange. Prices recovered on Wednesday, climbing back above $14,100 following the US midterm elections . The metal has now retreated from its September record of $14,875, raising questions about whether its historic rally is losing momentum. First, the recent AI stock market rout has shaken confidence in the spending boom behind new data centers. Copper is essential for electrical infrastructure, making it a popular investment tied to AI expansion. Marex analyst Ed Meir said copper appeared to be “catching up” with the recent semiconductor selloff. Second, Democrats’ victory in both chambers of Congress has reduced expectations of US tariffs on refined copper. Those tariff fears previously encouraged traders to stockpile copper in America, squeezing supplies elsewhere and pushing prices higher. Saxo Bank’s Ole Hansen warned that reduced tariff expectations could hurt copper prices. The surprising development is that physical copper demand remains relatively strong. China’s Yangshan copper premium, a measure of demand for imported metal, remains near $200 per ton, its highest in more than a decade. Meanwhile, Chinese warehouse inventories have fallen more than 75% in six months. Investors are selling copper over economic uncertainty while physical buyers continue competing for limited supplies. On the daily copper chart , prices remain in a descending channel after breaking their upward trendline. The $6.31-per-pound area is critical support, near July’s low. With energy prices elevated by the Middle East conflict, Australia is better placed than many importers, as LNG and coal export earnings help cushion a rising fuel bill. The data are unlikely to shift Reserve Bank of Australia expectations on their own, given the volatile gold component. Traders will look to upcoming volume data for a cleaner read on how much net exports are adding to growth. Gas and metals did the heavy lifting for Australia’s trade surplus in September, with a big drop in gold imports doing the rest. Australia’s goods trade surplus widened sharply in September to its largest in seven months, as a rise in exports of liquefied natural gas and metals coincided with a steep fall in gold imports, data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed on Thursday. The surplus on goods trade came in at about A$2.8 billion (around US$2 billion), up from A$184 million in August and well ahead of forecasts for a surplus of roughly A$1 billion or less. Exports rose 2.3% from the previous month, following a 3.7% gain in August. The increase was driven by other mineral fuels, a category that includes liquefied natural gas, and by metals, highlighting the support Australia’s resource sector continues to draw from global commodity demand. Imports fell 3.3%, reversing a 5.8% rise in August. The decline was led by gold, where imports dropped by nearly 35%. Gold flows can be volatile from month to month and often swing the headline balance, so the scale of the drop flatters the underlying improvement to some degree. The figures also suggest the recent rebound in fuel prices has yet to show up meaningfully in the import bill. As a large importer of refined fuel, Australia’s import costs would be expected to rise if higher prices persist, which could narrow the surplus in coming months. At the same time, higher energy prices tend to cut both ways for Australia. As a major exporter of liquefied natural gas and coal, the country benefits from elevated global energy prices on the export side, partly offsetting the cost of more expensive fuel imports. The stronger trade position is a positive for the economy’s external accounts, though its contribution to growth will depend on how the volume of trade, rather than its value, develops over the quarter. Attention now turns to whether commodity export strength can be sustained, and how quickly rising fuel costs feed into imports. Both will shape whether September proves a high point for the surplus or the start of a firmer trend. There's always something new to learn about the markets. body: The data offer something for both sides of the BoJ debate: historically sharp cost pressures support further tightening, while slowing hiring and weaker confidence give the cautious camp ammunition. On balance, the release is unlikely to shift December pricing materially, leaving the yen more sensitive to the BoJ minutes and oil-driven inflation signals. Firms citing inflation as a drag on confidence underlines how energy costs from the Middle East are feeding into Japanese business sentiment. Weak export orders point to limited support from overseas demand. Japan’s service providers are still growing and still paying up, but they’re hiring less and feeling gloomier about it. Japan’s services sector grew at a slightly faster pace in October, but a slowdown in manufacturing pulled overall private sector growth to a five-month low, while still-sharp cost pressures kept inflation in focus for the Bank of Japan, according to S&P Global’s latest survey. The S&P Global Japan Services PMI rose to 51.7 in October from 51.3 in September, marking a fifth straight month of expansion. Firms said stronger inflows of new work and efforts to broaden their customer base lifted activity, though growth remained modest and below the average so far this year. New orders also picked up slightly, driven by firmer domestic demand. Export business fell again, although the decline was the smallest in six months. Hiring was the weak spot. Services employment rose only marginally, the slowest pace in the current 14-month run of job creation, as some firms reported staff leaving through resignations and retirements. With capacity stretched, backlogs of work increased again. Price pressures slowed but stayed elevated. Input cost inflation fell to an eight-month low and output charges also rose more slowly, yet both remained well above their long-run averages. Business confidence about the year ahead dropped to its weakest since March, with firms citing inflation, an ageing population and labour shortages. The broader picture was softer. The composite PMI, which combines services and manufacturing, slipped to 52.1 from 52.3, its lowest since May, though it still pointed to a 19th consecutive month of growth. Faster services growth was offset by a slower rise in factory output. Across the private sector, job creation slowed to a one-year low and confidence fell to a three-month low. Input costs rose at a historically sharp rate, while growth in prices charged eased to a four-month low. S&P Global said input costs and selling prices, while rising more slowly, were still increasing at a pace that suggests official consumer inflation could stay elevated in the coming months. It added that whether growth loses further momentum and whether cost pressures ease will be key considerations for the BoJ as it weighs further tightening, warning that persistent inflation weighed on confidence and could also constrain demand and hiring. The data arrive on the same day as minutes from the BoJ’s September meeting, which showed policymakers agreed on the need for further rate increases, keeping attention on whether the central bank moves again in December. Korea bore the brunt. The exchange also said trading will open an hour late on November 19 to keep roads clear for the national university entrance exam. In Tokyo, the market divided along the same line. The broad Topix rose about 1.4%, led by real estate, retail and pharmaceuticals, while the tech-heavy Nikkei fell about 1.5% as chip equipment makers Advantest and Tokyo Electron slumped. Most Nikkei members rose, but losses in a handful of heavily weighted tech stocks dragged the index lower. Sony and Nintendo report after the close. SoftBank Group fell about 5.8% to around ¥4,020. body: What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… A majority of European Union citizens are in favor of an accelerated transition away from oil and gas and into alternative energy sources and transport electrification, a survey conducted by the European Investment Bank has shown, as reported by Reuters, which got an exclusive look at the survey. According to the survey, which involved 23,000 respondents, 87% wanted governments to make the transition a priority, with 52% saying solar should be at the top of the list of alternative, low-carbon energy sources. Nuclear, on the other hand, had only 19% saying it should be prioritized. The percentage in favor of wind as a top alternative energy source stood at 37%. “In a rapidly shifting geopolitical landscape, this is both the right thing to do for the planet and the smart thing to do for our economies, in order to bring down energy costs for businesses and households,” the president of EIB Group, Nadia Calvino, told Reuters. Calvino’s second point is interesting because over the past decade since the Paris Agreement was signed, the EU member states that spent the most on wind, solar, and electric vehicle support saw their electricity prices rise the most as well, while transition laggards have managed to keep bills relatively affordable. The war between the U.S., Israel, and Iran has highlighted the drawbacks of energy import dependence and strengthened the argument for locally sourced energy, especially from wind and solar installations, but also oil and gas where it is present. Proponents argue that both of these, especially solar, are already cheaper than gas generation. Critics note the cost estimates for wind and solar are based on levelized cost of energy metrics that exclude a lot of actual costs, such as the cost of electricity that needs to come from a baseload generator when there is no sun or, indeed, wind. summary: One policymaker voted to raise the bank's key interest rate to 4.25%.
body: The Bank of England announced its first interest rate hike in over three years on Thursday, raising its key rate by 25 basis points to 4%. The widely anticipated move marked the bank's first hike since Aug. 2023, and made it the last major central bank to embark on a tightening cycle since the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran eight months ago. The majority of the bank's Monetary Policy Committee voted for the quarter-point hike, with the motion passing by 8 votes to 1. The dissenting member voted to raise the bank's key interest rate by 50 basis points to 4.25%. "The conflict in the Middle East is now in its ninth month," the MPC said in a statement Thursday. "Global energy prices have continued to rise from an already elevated level." Policymakers said they now expected U.K. inflation to rise to "about 5%" by the middle of 2027. "It is then projected to fall as the impact of rising energy prices on 12-month inflation rates fades, and still restrictive monetary policy bears down on inflation," they said. Ahead of the decision being announced, markets had been pricing in more than a 99% chance of a rate hike, according to LSEG data. Traders were also pricing in a one-in-four chance of a further hike in December. Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said in the November Monetary Policy Report that without "real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East... risks to energy prices, and so to inflation, are to the upside." "Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach, dependent on the evidence on energy prices and inflation dynamics," he said. Data released earlier this month showed that the U.K.'s annual inflation rate jumped to 3.5% in September, driven by the surging cost of motor fuels. As a net energy importer, the U.K. is particularly vulnerable to external energy shocks — such as the one caused this year by the Iran war. The MPC's most hawkish member, Catherine L Mann, said she had voted for greater tightening than her peers because research pointed to "non-linear inflation risks." "My recent votes to increase Bank Rate by 25 basis points represented a 'down payment' to lean against second-round effects, reinforce credibility, and uphold 'good policy'," she said in comments published in the MPC's policy statement. "The economy has crossed the estimated statistical threshold into a high inflation-tight labour market regime where the asymmetric behavioural responses of households and firms support more robust second-round effects," Mann added. "A different research approach estimates that the economy may well have breached the policy credibility threshold, which worsens the policy trade-off... From a risk management and credibility perspective, a 50-basis point hike in Bank Rate is 'good policy'." Yields on U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, had been rising before the policy announcement and continued to edge higher after the Bank of England's update. The yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt was last seen 2 basis points higher at 5.1546%, while the 2-year gilt yield rose by 4 basis points to trade at 4.782%. The British pound , which hit a post-Brexit high on Wednesday, was flat against both the U.S. dollar and the euro on Thursday afternoon. Scott Gardner, investment strategist at JPMorgan Personal Investing, said in a note on Thursday that the November hike was "hugely symbolic." "The path ahead remains uncertain with much depending not only on how oil trades but also on natural gas prices which have risen sharply over the past few months. body: Bitcoin CME futures swept to $75,795 and rebounded on unusually heavy trading. The four-hour recovery is encouraging, but holding $79,040 and clearing $81,460 would tell us much more about whether buyers have genuinely regained control. Bitcoin CME futures have changed character in the space of a few sessions. After aggressive selling and repeated attempts to extend the decline, the market briefly broke below $76,000, recovered, and then rallied to $81,460 on November 4. It is a promising short-term reversal attempt, but the difference between a rebound and a lasting change of trend still matters. The starting point is straightforward: sellers achieved a fresh low but could not sustain the breakdown. Buyers then produced a much more decisive upward move. That echoes the lesson in Greg Michalowski's earlier Bitcoin analysis of sellers failing to extend a support break . His article examines different Bitcoin price references, so the levels in this CME futures analysis should be evaluated on their own terms. October 29: Sellers set the tone. CME Bitcoin futures traded as high as $82,270 before reversing. One four-hour candle fell from an $81,525 open to a $79,045 close. Another ended at $77,025 on volume of 4,141 contracts. There was no need to guess who had the advantage then: the price was moving substantially lower. October 30: Trading activity remained intense, but downside progress became less convincing. A four-hour candle traded between $76,550 and $78,200 on 4,576 contracts, yet opened at $77,425 and closed at $77,420, a net loss of just $5. That does not prove buyers were accumulating Bitcoin. It does show a great deal of trading without a meaningful change between the open and close. November 3: The break below the lows failed. A later four-hour candle fell to $75,795, undercutting earlier lows around $76,260-$76,450, then closed back at $77,905. This could have been a liquidity sweep , when a price move through a well-watched low triggers orders but fails to establish a new lower trading range. We can see the failed break in the price data; we cannot independently verify the stop orders or intentions behind it. November 4: Buyers finally generated meaningful upward displacement. A four-hour candle opened at $78,535, climbed to $81,460 and closed at $80,655, with volume of 5,468 contracts. That was about 5.1 times the preceding 20-bar average of 1,066 contracts. The comparison is striking, although the average includes thinly traded periods around the weekend, so the multiple should not be treated as a calibrated signal. By the last completed four-hour bar in the supplied November 5 snapshot, futures had closed at $80,925. The following bar was still developing. These are dated CME continuous-futures observations, not a live Bitcoin spot quote . Volume measures how much trading took place. It does not, by itself, tell us which side is winning. Compare the two unusually active four-hour candles. On October 30, 4,576 contracts accompanied a candle body of minus $5 . On November 4, 5,468 contracts accompanied a candle body of plus $2,120 . There was plenty of activity on both occasions, but only the second produced a decisive net change in price. The first pattern is consistent with buyers meeting aggressive selling or with two-sided trading. The second is stronger evidence that buyers were able to push prices higher. Neither observation proves institutional accumulation, trapped short positions or a particular order-flow mechanism. Concurrently, softening fundamentals weighed on the market, as JPMorgan reported a widening global oil supply surplus. Following the release of the U.S. midterm election results, in which the Democratic Party swept both the House of Representatives and the Senate, markets began betting that the Trump administration could face mounting pressure, potentially prompting the U.S. to reconsider military action against Iran. On November 4, WTI crude ( USOIL ) plunged intraday to as low as $87.13 per barrel, a decline of over 9.3%, while Brent crude ( UKOIL ) hit a low of $93.22 per barrel, down about 10%, marking its largest single-day drop since May. Heading into November 5, oil prices continued their downward trend, with WTI trading at $86.96 per barrel, down 1.24%, and Brent crude at $94.07 per barrel, down 0.57%. Brent has retreated more than 20% from its late-October high near $118, sinking to its lowest level in over two months. The Democratic victory reinforced market expectations of de-escalating warfare. U.S. Vice President Vance acknowledged that the monthslong war with Iran and the resulting surge in energy costs were key reasons for the Republican Party's midterm defeat. Democratic leaders, meanwhile, stated they would leverage Congress to push for an end to the conflict and constrain the Trump administration's tariff and military policies. With Democrats gaining control over budgets, hearings, and investigative powers, future military appropriations and operations could face stronger headwinds—a primary catalyst prompting traders to swiftly unwind crude oil risk premiums. However, market bets on a ceasefire may have run ahead of themselves. The new Congress will not be officially seated until January 2027, leaving Trump considerable diplomatic and military maneuverability until then. Even if Democrats can curtail certain military appropriations, the U.S. president retains broad executive authority in ongoing conflicts, and Congress can hardly halt military operations immediately. Trump could currently opt to maintain limited strikes, expedite negotiations, or re-escalate military action against Iran; any of these paths would keep oil prices highly volatile. Tehran has likewise signaled no clear concessions. Iran warned that shifts in the U.S. domestic political landscape do not necessarily translate into changes in its policy toward Iran, adding that it would mount an even larger-scale response if attacked again. Significant disagreements persist between the U.S. and Iran over the nuclear issue, sanctions relief, the unfreezing of overseas funds, and navigation arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz. Beyond political factors, global supply outstripping demand once again forms another key narrative driving oil prices lower. This indicates that the market has shifted from destocking to rebuilding inventories, stripping oil prices of the support previously provided by supply deficits. title: Wall Street surges after US midterms as oil prices tumble - CommBank
body: US stocks surged after the midterm elections ended Republican control of Congress, while oil prices tumbled and Treasury yields fell. US stocks soared on Wednesday after President Donald Trump's party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections. Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm US election, regardless of who wins, and the S&P 500 jumped 1.6% for its best day in three months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 3%, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.4%. Stocks of hospital owners and dollar stores serving low-income Americans helped lead the widespread rally following the nationwide losses for Republicans. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump's social-media company, the artificial-intelligence industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans. The price of Brent crude oil also tumbled below $US95 and touched its lowest level in two months. Vice President JD Vance blamed Republicans' midterm losses on the war with Iran, which caused a spike in oil prices. Strategists on Wall Street had been urging investors not to get swept up in the election because it may not matter much for the broad market in the long term. Prices for stocks depend more on where profits for companies and interest rates are heading than on who controls what in Washington. "Earnings trump elections," according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. Still, Wall Street may have got a preferred political scenario as Democrats are set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington because it lessens the risk of transformative changes to the economy. Much remains impossible to predict and Trump retains executive authority over key areas such as defence, foreign policy and, in some instances, trade. A downbeat forecast could be that "Trump is not now a lame duck, but an angry duck" who might restart tensions over tariffs and NATO allies' levels of military spending, said Carsten Brzeski, global chief of macro at ING Bank. An optimistic view, Brzeski said, is that Trump becomes "a tame duck ... that he will slow down any disruptive efforts and that he will put more focus on trying to win the Nobel Peace Prize by ending the two big wars without big disruption, and on trade, nothing happens but a few words." All told, the S&P 500 rose 119.70 points to 7,688.62. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 1,569.40 points to 53,356.12, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 364.50 points to 25,736.51. Trump's social-media company, Trump Media & Technology Group, was one of the market's bigger losers, down 24.5%. Since briefly touching a peak of $US175 five years ago, it's dropped to $US4.49. Its main business is Truth Social, which is most well known for Trump's postings on the platform. Elon Musk's businesses also struggled. Tesla fell 3.3%, and SpaceX sank 3.8%. Musk, a former top Trump adviser, is among the possible targets for investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress. Trump has been a big backer of the AI industry, and Democratic victories could mean more regulation or restrictions. Concerns have grown across political parties about AI in general. body: Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) will not exercise an option to more than double ​its existing agreement with AI cloud provider Nscale to rent more computing power at a Texas data center, Reuters reported on Thursday, citing a person familiar with the matter. The companies struck a deal last year for Nscale to deploy around 200,000 Nvidia (NVDA) AI chips with Microsoft ​across its data centers in Europe and the U.S. The reported development signals more pain for the IPO-bound Nscale. Last month, Microsoft pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's flagship data center project in ‌Essex, the UK, after ⁠power connection delays pushed its expected supply date into the 2030s. Nscale, backed by Nvidia, filed for an IPO in September, although a report last month said it faced opposition from investors over its $130 billion IPO valuation target. Reuters reported that Microsoft's decision to not expand the Texas contract was made ​several months ago, before Nscale filed for its IPO, and that its existing workflow, as per the original, was not affected. The development comes as the cloud industry faces increased scrutiny. In recent weeks, the debt-heavy model of neocloud firms such as CoreWeave has come under the scanner even as concerns prevail over overcapacity. The decisive midterm win by the Democrats, who are seen to be pro-AI regulation, has added concerns that new data centers will be harder and costlier to build. body: Wireless chipmaker Qualcomm QCOM beat Wall Street’s revenue expectations in calendar Q3 2026 (fiscal Q4 2026), but sales fell by 7.3% year on year to $10.44 billion. Guidance for next quarter’s revenue was optimistic at $10.8 billion at the midpoint, 2.6% above analysts’ estimates. Its non-GAAP profit of $2.17 per share was in line with analysts’ consensus estimates. Qualcomm’s recent quarter was met with a negative market reaction, as investors responded to declining year-over-year sales and a steep contraction in operating margins. Management identified ongoing headwinds in its core handset business, especially from memory pricing pressures and the loss of a major customer. CEO Cristiano Amon acknowledged, “The June quarter marked the low point for our China Android business, and we have seen sequential growth this quarter.” Licensing renewals with key partners like Apple and Huawei were cited as sources of stability amid ongoing industry volatility. Looking forward, Qualcomm’s guidance is built on expectations for strong growth in its non-handset segments, particularly automotive and data center. The company expects its custom silicon and AI accelerator products to drive significant revenue increases, while also forecasting that non-handset sales will account for over half of segment revenues in the coming year. CFO Akash Palkhiwala cautioned that ramping data center products will be “accretive to our operating margins, but dilutive to gross margins,” reflecting both opportunity and trade-offs as the business diversifies. Management attributed the quarter’s results to ongoing softness in handset demand, stabilization in licensing revenues, and the ramp-up of new business lines, particularly in automotive and data center. Qualcomm’s forward guidance reflects expectations for ongoing growth in automotive and data center, alongside persistent margin pressures as the business mix evolves.
